title: Why Your Taco Tuesday Might Cost More: Mexico's Food Prices Are Soaring!
summary: Have you ever gone to the store and noticed your favorite snacks cost more? In Mexico, families are feeling that pinch big time! At the Mercado de Abastos, a huge food market in Monterrey, prices for everyday foods like tomatoes, potatoes, beef, and chiles have shot up. Cesar Ramirez, a 66-year-old retiree, says, "You have to buy them anyway; they're things you use daily." But it's getting harder. Why? Fuel and fertilizer prices are rising worldwide because of shipping problems in a place called the Strait of Hormuz. That makes it more expensive to grow food and truck it to markets. Plus, some truck drivers and farmers are blocking roads to protest high costs and crime. Elvira Pasillas, a professor, says low-income families spend almost 70% of their money on food. That's like if you got $10 allowance and had to spend $7 just on lunch! Guillermina Delgado, a 62-year-old housewife, now buys only what she really needs each week. "There's not one single thing that is cheap anymore," she says. Beef prices jumped 16.5% in January alone. Mexico imports lots of gasoline from the U.S., so when global oil prices rise, everything costs more. The government is trying to help by cutting fuel taxes, but experts worry that might mean less money for other programs that help people. For now, many Mexican families are tightening their belts and hoping prices come down soon.
why_it_matters: When families in other countries struggle to afford food, it reminds us that the things we buy—like fruits and fuel—can depend on events far away, affecting our own snack prices and family budgets.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway in the Middle East through which a third of the world’s oil tankers pass. When tensions rise there, shipping gets disrupted, making fuel and goods more expensive worldwide.
Mexico buys much of its gasoline from the United States, so when oil prices rise globally, Mexican drivers pay more at the pump.
Monterrey, mentioned in the story, is a large industrial city in northern Mexico where the Mercado de Abastos is one of the biggest food markets.
